A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same torque-based motion-difficulty framework, despite retitling and renaming MDS to TVS. All 15 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original correlation and ablation results, curriculum-learning experiments, robot-transfer examples and flawed-motion analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds contact-force measurements, reward-perturbation experiments, hyperparameter sensitivity results and training-checkpoint analysis.

M1.justification: The three diversity components, weighted aggregation, K = 4, MID and DSJE formulas, and curriculum procedure are retained under the MDS-to-TVS rename. v2 newly specifies weights and contact-force omission, but does not establish a change to the underlying computational procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds GroundLink walking and hopping data for the contact-force sensitivity analysis in Section 4.2.1. AMASS imitation, inertial-mocap anomalies and Unitree G1 transfer were already covered in v1. Moving flawed-motion detection into the main text does not establish new coverage; AIST++ is mentioned only as a possible annotation target.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain UHC and PHC+, the PHC curriculum comparison against training without curriculum, and TWIST for G1 transfer. The new perturbation, hyperparameter and checkpoint analyses introduce no additional comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design: PHC+ rewards are measured under three increasing pose-perturbation levels for TVS < 150 and TVS > 350; UHC is used for weight and segment-count sweeps; PHC checkpoints are evaluated every 1,500 steps through 12,000. These are added protocols, while the existing AMASS and 9,000-episode curriculum settings remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test contact-force negligibility, the proposed flat-reward mechanism, sensitivity to integration weights and segment count, and whether MID tracks training progress (Section 4.2.1, Section 5.3, Appendices B.2–B.3). These materially broaden validation beyond the retained component ablations and existing application studies.

E5.justification: Both versions use Pearson, Spearman and Kendall correlations without reporting repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-test procedures. v2 adds effect-size interpretation and calls correlations significantly positive, but supplies no new uncertainty estimation or statistical test.

E6.justification: The original correlation, ablation, DSJE and curriculum tables retain identical numerical values. v2 adds contact-force measurements, hyperparameter correlations, perturbation rewards and a MID training curve. For example, Table 3 reports rewards falling from 263.99 to 224.75 for low-TVS motions versus 190.63 to 187.74 for high-TVS motions. These are new findings, not improvements on the original evaluations.

T1.justification: Section 4.2.1 adds an explicit approximation that contact-force derivatives are negligible relative to internal-dynamics derivatives, with a supporting argument. The scoring equations, MID/DSJE definitions and Appendix A propositions and proofs otherwise remain substantively unchanged. The stronger vanishing-gradient claims are not accompanied by a new formal proof.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds the first motion-difficulty definition and MD-AMASS benchmark. v2 explicitly describes AMASS scores as annotations rather than a new benchmark, and centers its contributions on distinguishing policy limitations from intrinsic learning constraints. It strengthens claims about vanishing gradients and principled error attribution, while promoting the existing anomaly-detection application into the main contribution narrative.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanatory argument through contact-force negligibility, reward plateauing as evidence of gradient starvation, parameter robustness and MID development during training. It also adds sensor-noise and actuator-limit qualifications to the previously computational limitations. Appendix B.3 overstates the new MID trend as monotonic despite Figure 7 showing a decrease from 302.5 to 299.5.

D1.justification: v2 discloses weights [0.4, 0.3, 0.3], explains contact-force omission, and states that scores and the computation pipeline are publicly released, without supplying an access link. Conversely, it drops v1's explicit 30-FPS description and scatter-plot outlier-filter disclosure. RBDL, hardware and runtime information remain; the omitted disclosure does not establish a changed filter.

R1.justification: The related-work survey largely retains the same literature. v2 adds GroundLink and invokes Winter and Cohen for its new arguments, while narrowing the novelty positioning of AMASS annotation. The citation-style conversion and expanded bibliographic metadata are presentation changes.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are extensively rewritten around diagnosis rather than benchmarking. Terminology changes throughout from MDS to TVS, Sections 4–6 are reframed, and flawed-motion detection moves from Appendix C.3 to Section 6.3. These constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration, removes the AMASS segmentation diagram, adds motion examples to the main scatter plots, and relocates flawed-motion visualization into the main text. It adds reward and sensitivity tables and a MID trajectory plot, while extensively reformatting the appendices into a single-column layout.

improvement.justification: The added sensitivity studies, reward-response evidence, disclosed weights and practical limitations modestly strengthen support for the retained metric. The main results and proofs remain unchanged. Benefits are tempered by removing the outlier-filter disclosure, leaving perturbation magnitudes and sample sizes unspecified, and incorrectly describing Figure 7's MID trajectory as monotonic. The additions therefore support a limited overall gain rather than fully validating the stronger error-attribution claims.
